title: Al-Amin, the trustworthy
hookLine: a young shepherd and merchant becomes known in Mecca as the one you leave your valuables with

cards: House keys make a good test. Not a phone password: the actual keys to your home, handed over for a month while you're away. That list tends to be short, one or two names, if that.
In Mecca, one young man's name sat on that kind of list all over town. Not rich, not powerful, an orphan raised by his uncle. You met his nickname on day twenty of this path: al-Amin.
The trustworthy one. Today, the word behind it.

teach.h: AMANAH: A TRUST, GIVEN BACK WHOLE.
teach.b: The word is amanah: a trust. Something handed to you that isn't yours, to keep safe and give back whole. Money left in your care, a secret, a job, a promise.
It comes from the root a-m-n, to be safe, secure.
The same root gives iman, faith, and amin, the trustworthy. In Arabic, faith, safety and trustworthiness are family. How did he earn the name?
Not with speeches. As a boy he herded sheep for Meccan families for a few coins; a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says he told his companions every prophet had been a shepherd.
As a young man he traveled with the trade caravans.
The name stuck so hard that, years later, even people in Mecca who opposed him kept leaving their valuables with him.

The seerah says that on the night he finally left Mecca, he asked his cousin 'Ali to stay behind and return every deposit to its owner. Even his opponents' things. The Qur'an makes this a command for everyone.
In Pickthall's translation: “Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners.” And it goes further.
It describes the amanah being offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they shrank from carrying it. The human being took it on.
Muslim scholars read that trust in many ways: faith, the body, time, the earth itself. In that reading, everything a person holds is held on loan.

how: Muslims treat keeping trusts, returning loans, keeping secrets and keeping promises as part of faith itself, and a hadith lists betraying a trust among the signs of a hypocrite.

o: a gift that becomes yours to keep
a trust, kept safe and given back whole
faith, the belief you hold in your heart

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: even people who opposed him left valuables with him
and the seerah says 'Ali stayed behind to return them when he left.
amanah only means money left in your care
it's any trust: money, a secret, a job, a promise, and in 33:72, the great trust humans took on.
faith and trust share a root in Arabic
a-m-n gives iman, faith, and amanah, trust.

games.q: the Prophet is leaving Mecca in secret, at night, with his life in danger. he still holds valuables that belong to people who want him dead. what does he do?
o: leave someone behind to return them all.
games.why: the seerah says he left 'Ali behind to give every deposit back to its owner.

practice: Think of one promise that's still open: a call, a thing you borrowed, a deadline, an I'll be there at six. Picture keeping it exactly, not roughly, not late, not almost, but on time and whole, and decide when you'll do it.
If you pray, you can ask Allah to make you trustworthy in small things.

wordCard.voice: Amanah. A trust: whatever is placed in your care, to be kept safe and given back whole. The root of al-Amin, the Prophet's name in Mecca.

orig.note: Arabic: a trust; from a-m-n, to be safe.

carryVoice: Your line: be the one they trust. Tomorrow, a businesswoman in Mecca notices him. Until then.
